(2) A genuine engine inconsistency that is a permission-free-to-set-up but permission-gated-to-read zoom oracle: ScreenDetailed.devicePixelRatio is the bare device scale factor while window.devicePixelRatio is that value times the page zoom, so dividing one by the other yields the exact zoom level. A patch that pins LocalDOMWindow::devicePixelRatio to a constant fails three ways at once: the CSS `resolution` feature still reads the real product, the DPR client hint on subresources still reads the real product, and the ratio stops responding to zoom, which no real browser does. verdict_reason: Window size is user state, not device identity. A real user's window is whatever size they dragged it to, so there is no single correct value to replay and any fixed value is itself anomalous — a population of sessions all reporting one exact outer size is a stronger signal than any individual size. What must be true is a RELATION, not a value: the window rect must fit inside the claimed available rect (coh.window-within-avail-rect) and its distance from innerHeight must match the claimed OS's browser furniture (coh.window-chrome-inset-matches-os). Both are enforced by sizing the real OS window at launch, which keeps the value produced by the code path that would have produced it (A1), rather than by patching an accessor.

The failure mode this row guards against is a profile claiming a 1728x1117 display while running maximised on a 2560x1440 host: outerWidth 2560 against screen.width 1728 is arithmetically impossible and decides the session on its own.

verdict_reason: A client rect is the output of a real layout, not a stored attribute — the same class of value as a canvas render. It is correct when its INPUTS are correct (font set, font rasterisation, zoom factor, device scale factor, scrollbar width), and there is no value to replay because the rect depends on the document being measured. More importantly, the measured competitor artifact proves that perturbing it is strictly worse than leaving it: noise here is quantised to 1/64 px by LayoutUnit and has no natural cause, so it converts an ordinary value into a positive identification of tampering. The emitters are listed so that they are recognisably OFF-LIMITS, not so that they can be patched.

evidence.note: LayoutUnit stores multiples of 1/64 px in int32; kFixedPointDenominator = 1 << kFractionalBits. This is why the competitor's offsets were 1/64 and 2/64 and could not have been anything else

a competing browser returned x=-10000.015625 and y=-0.03125 for the same stylesheet

The invariant is that a rect must equal what the layout produced, which for integer-declared positions is an integer and for text-driven positions is a multiple of 1/64. the feature is cumulative: a P3 display answers true to both srgb and p3, a BT2020 display to all three

notes: corpus_coverage derivable rather than present: the capture records which buckets matched, but the value the browser actually holds is an ICC profile, and the bucket does not determine it. The patch therefore installs a colour space rather than writing an answer — which is correct anyway, because a bare bucket write would leave the colour space disagreeing with the gamut and would not move screen.colorDepth or dynamic-range, which come from the same object. Note the HDR short-circuit means an HDR display can never report srgb-only, so colorDepth 30 with color-gamut srgb is an impossible combination.

evidence.note: `standard` returns true unconditionally; `high` returns MediaValues::DeviceSupportsHDR()
DeviceSupportsHDR is ScreenInfo::display_color_spaces.SupportsHDR()
video-dynamic-range is documented in-tree as making no distinction from dynamic-range and returns the same answer
the browser strips HDR out of every ScreenInfo before sending when hardware acceleration is unavailable
dynamic-range ['standard','high']

notes: The same HDR bit as screen.colorDepth 30 and the color-gamut P3 short-circuit, read a third way. Because RenderWidgetHostImpl::GetVisualProperties disables HDR when hardware acceleration is off, this row is coupled to the GPU configuration owned by subsystem 5: a profile claiming an HDR display cannot be run with software rendering, and that is a launch-configuration constraint rather than a patch.

verdict_reason: This feature is viewport orientation, not display orientation: it compares the viewport width against the viewport height and nothing else. It therefore carries no display identity, follows automatically from window.inner-dimensions, and must NOT be tied to screen.orientation.type — a window taller than it is wide on a landscape monitor legitimately reports portrait here and landscape-primary there, in stock Chrome.

evidence.note: `double width = *media_values.Width(); double height = *media_values.Height();` then width > height means landscape; a square viewport is classified as portrait
orientation ['landscape'] with innerWidth 1728 > innerHeight 913 — consistent with the viewport rule, and coincidentally also with the landscape screen

notes: Recorded specifically to prevent a false coherence edge. The obvious-looking constraint 'CSS orientation must equal screen.orientation.type' is wrong and enforcing it would introduce a difference from stock Chrome rather than remove one. The square-viewport-is-portrait rule is also worth knowing: it is a Chromium choice, not a spec requirement, and differs from some other engines.

observable: the DPR / Sec-CH-DPR request header sent on navigation and subresource requests once an origin opts in via Accept-CH

evidence.note: AddDPRHeader runs in the BROWSER process and computes device_scale_factor * zoom_factor from display::Screen::Get()->GetPrimaryDisplay().device_scale_factor() and HostZoomMap — it never consults the renderer
the RENDERER writes the same header on subresource requests from Document::DevicePixelRatio() = LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio(), an entirely separate computation
`dpr: 2` observed on the wire alongside window.devicePixelRatio 2 — the header is real, not hypothetical

notes: THE deviceMemory FAILURE, REPEATED EXACTLY, and the strongest argument in this shard for patching in the browser process. One header name, two independent producers split by request type: the browser computes it for the navigation, the renderer for every subresource. A renderer-only patch to LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio changes JavaScript, CSS and the subresource header while leaving the navigation header carrying the host's real ratio — a server sees a document whose HTML request said one thing and whose image requests say another, which is cheaper to check than any JavaScript probe. Two further stock divergences the patch must reproduce rather than fix: the browser uses the PRIMARY display's scale factor while the renderer uses the display the window is on, and the browser uses the host zoom map's zoom while the renderer uses the frame's composed layout zoom.

observable: the Viewport-Width / Sec-CH-Viewport-Width and Sec-CH-Viewport-Height request headers
verdict_reason: These headers report the viewport, and the viewport is user state for the same reasons window.inner-dimensions is: there is no device-identity value to replay. They become correct when the window is sized coherently with the claimed screen. Recorded rather than dropped because they are produced by two different processes and can therefore disagree with window.innerWidth in a way no in-page probe would reveal.

evidence.note: the browser takes view->GetVisibleViewportSize() from its own RenderWidgetHostView and divides by the HostZoomMap zoom factor
the renderer takes LocalFrameView::ViewportWidth()/ViewportHeight() (local_frame_view.cc:4527,4532), which are the layout size adjusted for absolute zoom — the same quantity as window.innerWidth
`viewport-width: 1728` observed on the wire on a same-origin fetch, exactly equal to the measured window.innerWidth of 1728

notes: The T0 capture shows the header equalling innerWidth exactly on a subresource request, which is the invariant to hold. The interesting case is the navigation request, where the value comes from the browser's view bounds and its own zoom map rather than from the renderer's layout — under a non-default zoom or during a resize the two producers can disagree, and a server comparing the navigation header against a subresource header sees it. Not spoofed, but it is a reason the profile loader must not set browser-side and renderer-side zoom independently.
